opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the next direction comes down to a few things.

The first is moving from solving problems to doing mathematics. Competition problems were a useful proving ground because they're well-posed, have known answers, and let you measure progress. But real mathematical work looks different. You don't know whether a statement is true. You have to formulate the right conjectures, build up definitions, and find the lemmas that make a long argument go through. So we're increasingly interested in systems that can explore and propose, not only answer.

The second is verification, which for us means formal methods. Natural-language proofs from a model can look very convincing and still contain a subtle gap. If you want mathematicians to actually trust and use what an AI produces, the output needs to be checkable. That's why we care so much about formal languages like Lean. A proof that compiles in a proof assistant is a different kind of object from a proof that merely reads well. Formal verification also gives you a clean reward signal, which matters a lot for training.

The third is what I'd call the data and library problem. Formal mathematics is still a tiny corpus compared to all the mathematics humans have written down. A big part of the work ahead is autoformalization: translating informal mathematics into formal statements and proofs at scale, carefully enough that the formal statement actually means what the paper meant. That's harder than it sounds, because misformalizing a theorem can quietly turn it into something trivial or false.

Finally, I think the long-term picture is collaboration rather than replacement. The most exciting outcome isn't a system that wins a medal. It's one a working mathematician can hand a messy idea to, which comes back with "here's a counterexample," or "here's a formal proof of the lemma you were stuck on," or "here's a connection to another field you might not have seen." If we can get there, mathematics itself could change, in how fast ideas get tested and in how much of the field one person can reach.

And mathematics matters beyond itself. It's the cleanest testbed for reasoning we have, because truth there is unambiguous. Whatever we learn about building systems that reason reliably and verifiably in math, I expect will carry over to code, to science, and to other places where getting it right really matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that we're moving away from treating math as a benchmark to beat and toward treating it as a place where a model actually has to do research, not just answer questions.

For the past couple of years the field was organized around competition problems. Those were useful because they had clean, verifiable answers, and that let us build the reinforcement learning loops that got us to where we are. But competition math is a closed world. Somebody already knows the answer, the problem has been curated to be solvable in a few hours, and the hard part was really just search and verification under a time limit. Once the models cleared that bar, it stopped telling us much.

So the next direction for us has three pieces.

The first is formalization at scale. We want the model to work inside proof assistants like Lean so that every step is machine-checked rather than graded by a human reading a natural-language proof. That removes the trust problem. A proof is either accepted by the kernel or it isn't. And it changes how the model learns, because the environment can give feedback on every intermediate step instead of only on the final answer.

The second is open problems rather than curated ones. We've been building a pipeline where the model generates conjectures, tries to prove or refute them, and then we have mathematicians look at the ones that survive. The interesting output isn't necessarily a famous conjecture being resolved. It's the thousands of small lemmas and counterexamples that nobody bothered to write down because they weren't worth a human's week. That's where I think the near-term value is for working mathematicians.

The third piece, and the one I care most about, is collaboration rather than autonomy. The question I get asked constantly is when the model will replace mathematicians. I think that's the wrong framing. The best interactions we've seen are where a mathematician has a vague intuition, the model turns it into something precise, finds the gap, and the human redirects. Neither one could do it alone at that speed. So we're spending a lot of effort on the interface, on how the model explains why an approach failed, and on making it humble about what it hasn't verified.

If I had to compress it: less about scores, more about proof objects, and more about being a good colleague to people who already know what they're doing.

astra-6.text:
I think the next direction is to move from solving individual problems toward developing methods that transfer across problems. Getting an answer is one milestone, but we also want to understand which ideas made the solution possible and whether those ideas can help somewhere else.

That means paying attention to the process: how to choose a useful representation, when to try a simpler case, and how to recognize that an approach has reached a dead end. I’d like our work to make those decisions more systematic while still leaving room for exploration. Ideally, each problem we solve should teach us something about how to approach the next one.
